questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] choosing idempotency over an outbox: when NOT to build the heavier machinery (masteropen, openstatus/fabledocs3/adr-009-idempotency-over-outbox.md). An uptime-monitoring product probes 20,000 monitors every minute from 6 regions, so about 2,000 probe results a second come back to one status endpoint; a monitor's global status flips when enough regions agree, an incident opens, and pages go out through Slack, PagerDuty, SMS and email providers. Fan-out runs on a managed task queue that retries, every provider call is retried, and the team of three runs no message broker of its own. Write your design before you look: what you rely on instead of transactions at each step, which steps can live with idempotent identity alone and which cannot, what each idempotency key is made of, how two regions reporting at once are kept from double- or zero-paging, how an outage ends, and what you are choosing not to build. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Start from the boundary: no transaction can span the task queue and the notification vendors, and every layer retries, so idempotent identity is the floor whatever else is built; even an outbox would still lean on provider-side dedupe keys to absorb its dispatcher's duplicates.
keyPoints.quote: Full transactionality is impossible across those boundaries

keyPoints.text: [w3] Each step is judged by which failure costs the product more. Where a repeated effect is harmless, identity alone is enough; for paging, a customer who hears nothing is worse off than one notified twice, so any write-and-send ordering that can drop a notification is ruled out there, even though fixing it means accepting repeats.
keyPoints.quote: For a paging product, at-least-once with dedupe is the defensible default

keyPoints.text: [w3] Every key's parts are chosen on purpose and written down (for example monitor, region and tick for a probe task; notification, monitor and tick for a page), because a key that is too coarse swallows real events and one that is too fine lets duplicates through, and neither shows up as an error.
keyPoints.quote: idempotency-key granularity is a silent correctness parameter

keyPoints.text: [w2] Two regions reporting the same monitor at once are serialized on purpose, not left to luck: either one transaction around the status flip, the incident and the page record, or the status endpoint's work keyed per monitor on the queue.
[w2] Per-region results are stored as evidence and only a quorum of them flips the global verdict, so a single flapping region cannot page anyone.
[w2] An outage ends by compensation: the open incident is closed and flagged as auto-resolved, never rolled back or deleted, so the record of what customers saw stays true.
[w1] The saving is named: no broker or dispatcher to deploy, scale and watch, which is the cost the idempotency-only design avoids.
keyPoints.quote: the pipeline needs no broker of its own

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — customers report a 40-minute outage and no page at all. During it the workflows service was OOM-killed in the middle of a status update, the database returned errors for a few seconds, two regions reported the same failing tick at the same moment, and the scheduler re-invoked the probe cron after a slow response. The dashboards show no failed sends. What broke, how does each problem show, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Killed after the global status was written as error but before the incident insert: the retried report reads a monitor that is already in error and returns before any incident or page record exists, so the untransacted status flip is a gate that loses the page by itself, ahead of any page dedupe.

[w3] The page-record insert treats every error as a duplicate: its catch does not check for a unique violation, so a transient database error skips the send while the log says the trigger already exists.
[w3] Two regions reporting at once each read the state from before the flip, so both act on it or each assumes the other did, which ends in a duplicate page or a missing one.
keyPoints.quote: two regions reporting concurrently can both read pre-flip state

keyPoints.text: [w2] Task names embed the time the cron handler itself started (Date.now(), folded into the name at cron/checker.ts:336), so the no-op only covers retries inside one run; a re-invoked cron mints new names and enqueues the whole tick again, and only the status check, with its own race, keeps that from paging twice.
[w2] Nothing records whether a provider accepted a page, so a page lost to dedupe and a monitor with no channels configured look the same, and 'no failed sends' proves nothing.
keyPoints.quote: the schema records that a trigger existed, not that a provider accepted the page

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend the decision against the alternatives the ADR itself names: a transactional outbox, send-then-record, the lighter send-status-plus-sweep path, and wrapping the status flip in a transaction versus serializing it per monitor; then say when idempotent identity alone really is the right amount of machinery, and what the quorum rule costs. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] The outbox was rejected for its moving parts (a dispatcher, an intent table to drain and watch); that is a good reason only while the failure it removes is minor, and silent loss of the product's core promise is not minor, which is why the ADR calls this the decision most worth revisiting.

[w3] Send-then-record buys no lost pages at the price of a duplicate page after a crash; a duplicate is visible and survivable while a suppressed page is silent, so for a paging product the loud failure is the one to keep.
keyPoints.quote: the failure mode chosen instead (silent suppression) is strictly worse for this product

keyPoints.text: [w2] Before the full outbox there is a lighter step: a send status on the existing page record plus a retry sweep keeps the dedupe identity already in place and adds no new deployable, with the outbox kept for gaps that record cannot see.
keyPoints.quote: send status on the trigger row + a retry sweep, or a real outbox

keyPoints.text: [w3] A transaction around flip, incident and page record fixes the race in the database but relies on isolation the team already distrusts over its HTTP database driver; keying the status work per monitor on the queue serializes it without that trust, at the cost of per-monitor throughput and queue configuration.
keyPoints.quote: the quorum flip is a read-check-write across awaits

keyPoints.text: [w2] Identity alone is the right amount of machinery when the system that performs the effect also enforces the key, as the queue does for a named task; it stops being enough when the dedupe record and the effect are two separate writes in two systems.
keyPoints.quote: Cloud Task names are derived deterministically, so double-enqueue is a no-op

keyPoints.text: [w1] Structural anti-flapping needs no tuned delay, but the threshold is a design choice: in the code a flip needs at least half of a monitor's regions, so on an even region count a tie flips, and a one-region monitor flips on a single report.
